title: The hypertrophy series: using lifting rotations to maximize quality tonnage
summary: Lifting rotations must sit within a range of specificity: pick a main lift per muscle (e.g. bench for chest), rotate its variations and complementary movements, keep tonnage roughly constant across sessions dedicated to that muscle, and optionally sprinkle small accessory tonnage on other days. Too few lifts limits control of volume/intensity; too many creates 'mayhem' where techniques never get practiced enough.

claims.claim: The principle of specificity matters for bodybuilders, less than for powerlifters, but must still be respected, and lifting rotations are tied to it.
Your ability to rotate lifts while keeping tonnage constant depends on smart exercise selection.
If the bench is your main chest builder, your rotation should include bench variations and other lifts that complement it by working the chest.
Having a strength focus on one exercise is good, but you don't have to do only its variations (close grip, Spoto press, board/pin presses); you can branch out to any movement targeting the muscle.
Within a muscle's lift selection, some movements carry most of the tonnage and others are much lighter; that range makes volume and intensity easier to control.
Too large a range (e.g. 55 chest lifts) is confusing, prevents training each movement often enough and is detrimental; too much minimalism is also bad, so strike a balance.
Sessions dedicated to a muscle should have similar tonnage; a chest day with a third of the tonnage of another chest day is a bad idea, though one slightly higher is fine.
You can add easy-to-warm-up accessory work for a muscle on a non-dedicated day (push-ups, ring push-ups, flies for chest on arm day); you don't have to respect a body part split 100%.
Slapping extra volume on a non-dedicated day increases frequency, brings blood to the muscle, aids recovery and adds some tonnage; not a revolution, but natural bodybuilding is stacking pebbles.
Bodybuilders shouldn't be jacks of all trades: doing dips, weighted dips, bench and weighted push-ups all for chest diverts attention unless you're a chest specialist.

Applying very high exercise selection to every muscle creates mayhem: you can't practice each lift enough within one or two weeks, technique suffers and tonnage becomes unstable as you keep relearning lifts.
Pick your favorite movements that work for you, milk them with strength work, and use specific variations of them to add tonnage.
Seemingly technical concepts like lifting rotations and specificity do apply to bodybuilding because they directly affect tonnage.
